title: AI Strategist: Readiness and Transformation
description: Domain 4 (24%): readiness and maturity, AWS CAF, data foundations, sponsors and champions, culture and AI literacy, and scaling from pilot to enterprise with a CoE.

cards.definition: Checking leadership alignment, data quality, cultural preparedness, technical infrastructure, and governance before scaling AI, to find the gap that will actually block it.

example.text: A survey finds leaders keen on AI agents, yet only 13% rate their data ready, 11% their governance, and 5% their workforce. The gaps, not the technology, are the blocker.

cards.definition: AWS guidance that groups the capabilities behind a successful transformation into six perspectives: Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security, and Operations.
Naming what is missing across people, process, technology, and governance that stops an AI program moving forward, so investment goes to the real gap.
AWS's four-level model (Envision, Experiment, Launch, Scale) for placing an organization; each aspect is assessed separately and no level is inherently better.
Building awareness, exploring use cases, and assessing cultural readiness and governance needs, with no formal AI projects or budget yet.
Running structured pilots and proofs of concept with small cross-functional teams to validate business value and build core skills and governance.
Putting a few proven AI applications into production with risk, governance, and responsible-AI policies, monitoring, and operations and support teams.
Many AI applications across departments, built from reusable components and self-service platforms, with a formal operating model, RACI, and automated governance.

example.text: A dozen teams at a bank launch new AI apps from a shared library of approved patterns through an internal portal, instead of each starting from scratch.

cards.definition: The CAF for AI's four repeating stages: Envision, Align, Launch, Scale. Its second stage is Align (capabilities, stakeholders), not the maturity model's Experiment.
The incremental plan for moving up a maturity level: an AI roadmap and data strategy, alignment with business goals, investment in talent and tools, and governance.

example.text: An Envision-level firm moves up by forming cross-functional squads, shortlisting its top use cases, securing budget for small proofs of concept, and defining success metrics for each.

cards.definition: Whether the data a use case needs exists, is good enough in quality, and can be reached by the people and systems that need it.
Data held in systems or departments where others cannot easily reach or share it, which lowers its value and leads to duplicates, errors, and manual work.

example.text: Customer history sits in a legacy billing system and a separate sales tool that do not talk to each other. Reports conflict and staff copy data by hand until the systems are integrated.

cards.definition: The plan for which data an organization collects, curates, governs, and shares to fuel AI; CAF-AI calls it what keeps the AI flywheel in motion.
A data-sharing model where each business domain owns its data and serves it to others as a product, under organization-wide standards and federated governance.
Sets policy for a dataset: who may access it and when, how regulations apply, and what key terms mean.
A business-side role that applies data governance day to day in projects, spots data issues, monitors compliance, and escalates problems.
Amazon Bedrock is the fully managed, serverless default, with RAG, safeguards and customization built in; Amazon SageMaker AI is for models Bedrock lacks or more control over hosting and training.

example.text: A team that only needs answers from existing models starts on Bedrock. A team that must train its own model moves to SageMaker AI, accepting more operational work for more control.

cards.definition: AWS's four-layer approach: reliable infrastructure, foundation model selection, security and governance, and repeatable application patterns.
A senior leader whose support champions the AI program from the top, backed by clear leadership roles for decision-making and accountability.
People inside the organization, identified early, who lead the exploration of AI opportunities in their own areas and keep momentum going.
A small team with clear roles mixing business, IT, security and governance, and AI experts; AWS sees it as the forerunner of a formal AI CoE.
A chart naming who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each AI activity; a first version is signed off at Launch and formalized at Scale.
One named person accountable for the business result of an AI initiative, not just for deploying it.
Telling the workforce openly what AI will change, when, what outcomes to expect, and how roles and job security are affected, including upskilling plans.
Risk aversion, resistance to change, and fear of failure; leaders respond by making it safe to question assumptions, experiment, and learn new skills.

example.text: A firm trains its existing staff rather than hiring an elite AI team. It builds talent that knows the business and eases the fear of people worried about their jobs.

cards.definition: Built-up outdated processes, rigid hierarchies, too many approval layers, and resistance to change; adding AI on top compounds it rather than transforming the business.
A shared basic understanding of AI across the organization, from the C-suite down, so people can spot real uses and discuss AI in common terms.
Small, limited-scope builds on real use cases with clear success metrics, used to test business value and give teams hands-on AI experience.
A short internal event where teams try AI hands-on, used to encourage experimentation and foster innovation.
Training people on the organization's ethical and responsible-AI guidelines alongside technical skills, so they can apply them in their work.
Augmentation uses AI to help a person do each step better; automation hands the step to AI. Much of AI's gain may come from empowering people rather than replacing steps.
As AI takes routine tasks, people move to solving problems and checking AI output for accuracy, and managers move from task oversight to mentoring and quality assurance.

example.text: Claims handlers stop keying data and instead review AI-drafted decisions, judging when to trust the draft and when to step in.

cards.definition: Critical thinking, empathy, and creativity: the human strengths the exam guide says to balance against AI capabilities when redesigning roles.
Early, visible AI successes that build faith in the program and help people see where else AI could help; a base for scaling up.
Weariness from funding pilots that never reach production, which can stifle innovation and discourage further experimentation with AI.
Proven AI capabilities and patterns packaged so other teams can reuse them, letting one success spread across business units at low extra cost.

example.text: A search-and-summarize tool built for a product research team is reused by legal for due diligence, by auditors to surface risks, and by sales for buyer research.

cards.definition: A dedicated unit that guides AI across the organization with best practices and shared technical capabilities, working with business units to find opportunities.

example.text: An AI unit set up far from the C-suite, with incentives not tied to the business or customers, drifts into work with no business value, a common mistake CAF-AI warns about.

cards.definition: A centralized CoE coordinates and runs AI work from one unit; a federated one keeps a small central team for shared standards while business units run their own.
A live view combining AI costs (cost per interaction, infrastructure spend) with value (hours saved, revenue lift, CSAT); AWS calls it a primary production artifact.
Feeding monitoring results and user feedback back into regular improvements, because a live AI application is a living system whose value can degrade.
What must be in place before go-live: governance and responsible-AI policies, monitoring and alerts, a human-in-the-loop process, SLAs, and support teams.
Preproduction hardens, tests, and de-risks (load, security, compliance); production shifts the goal to steady user value, strategic goals, and clear ROI.
